topic: What if you could pause everyone but you?
title: WHAT IF YOU COULD
PAUSE EVERYONE BUT YOU?

power.rule: one tap and everything but you stops — rain, traffic, friends, even light
power.look: a cold PAUSED grade, a blinking PAUSED chip, the world still while Pip moves through it

script.text: Dusk rain. Pause. Two hundred drops, frozen. Walk them dry.
Football at your face. Pause. Catch it slow.
Mo on his phone. Pause. Steal his snack. He'll never know.
What if you could pause everyone but you?
One tap. Everyone stops, mid-step, mid-laugh, mid-argument. Except you.
The test you didn't study for? Pause. Twenty minutes of thinking, one school second.
Mum, midsentence, finger up. Grab the toast. Unpause. Normal morning.
Your sister's ice cream, mid-fall. Pause. Catch. Hand it back. Her face: priceless.
The world runs on your clock now.

script.beat: 4 the not-so-fun part: the cost, one real fact
4 the fact, worked out on the board
script.text: Light crosses a room in ten nanoseconds. Paused there, it never lands. If your power took the light with everything else, you'd tap, and go blind. That's real.
So your pause keeps one exception: light already inside your eyes.
But your rule has a hole. Yesterday, midpause, you weren't alone. A charcoal suit walked between the frozen kids.
He stopped. He looked straight at you. Then he checked a stopwatch — like he was timing your taps.
Today the corridor pauses, like always. You take your shortcut. Then you see him. Standing at your sister.
Sis, mid-giggle, frozen. His hand, two steps from her shoulder.
You can't run. Unpause, and ten thousand people see him too.
So who else is walking around in your pause? Part 1.

science.claim: Even light freezes: light crosses a room in ten nanoseconds, so paused in flight it never lands — if the power froze the world's light, you'd go blind in the instant you tap.
science.working: A room is about 3 m across; light moves at c = 299,792,458 m/s, so 3 m / c = 1.00e-8 s = 10 ns. If everything but you stops, photons in flight stop where they are: the last photon that was ever going to reach your eye is already inside it, and none of the frozen ones ever complete the remaining fractions of a millimetre. Sight needs a continuous stream of new photons (daylight puts ~1e14 photos/s on the pupil; the threshold is ~90). So a world-pause that took the light would leave the frozen scene as your final frame. Pip's power must therefore have an unspoken exception: the pause spares light already inside his eyes — which is also why the man in the suit is the scary question in beat 5.
science.source: c = 299,792,458 m/s (BIPM, SI definition); eye photon flux: Hecht, Shlaer & Pirenne 1942 (threshold ~90 photons), typical daylight pupil flux ~1e14 photons/s

science.claim: Sound freezes too — paused air can't carry a pressure wave, so inside the pause you'd be deaf as well.
science.working: Sound is molecules handing a push along: a 3 m room at 343 m/s takes ~9 ms. Frozen molecules pass nothing on, so the pause is total silence from the first instant — and no wind, no draft, no echo while it holds.
science.source: Speed of sound in air, 343 m/s at 20 C (standard acoustics reference)

science.claim: 'Twenty minutes of thinking, one school second': your own time keeps running inside the pause while the world doesn't spend any.
science.working: The pause exempts you, so your clock — including your reaction and thought time — runs on while everyone else's is suspended. Twenty minutes of your private time passes in a school second for everyone else; the school day never loses a second.
science.source: arithmetic on the power's stated rule ('everyone but you')
